world.title: Somalia's Senate Unanimously Passes Anti
world.desc: MOGADISHU — Somalia’s Upper House of Parliament has unanimously approved the Anti-Piracy and Anti-Kidnapping Bill, with 29 senators voting in favor and none against, excluding the chairperson who presided over the session. The bill, which was previously passed by the House of the People, now awaits presidential assent from President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud. Once signed into law, it will strengthen Somalia’s legal framework to combat piracy and kidnapping amid a renewed wave of attacks off the country’s coast. The approval comes as Somali piracy has seen a dramatic resurgence in 2026, with at least eight hijackings since April, including two within a fortnight in August. The attacks have been driven by a convergence of factors, including the diversion of international naval resources to counter Houthi threats in the Red Sea and the war on Iran, which has created a security vacuum that pirates are exploiting. Strengthening the Legal Framework The revised Anti-Piracy and Anti-Kidnapping Law updates legislation first enacted in 1975, modernizing legal tools to address contemporary maritime threats. The updated law includes clearer definitions of piracy and kidnapping, expanded jurisdiction over maritime crimes, stronger penalties ranging from 5 to 20 years in prison, and improved legal procedures to ensure fair investigations and trials. The legislation also aligns Somalia’s legal framework with international standards, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) and the Djibouti Code of Conduct, strengthening Somalia’s ability to cooperate with international partners in prosecuting maritime crimes. According to the Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs, which submitted the bill, the legislation represents a “pivotal step” in strengthening maritime security, protecting vital trade routes, and ensuring the safety of Somali citizens.
